title: Conway's Law and the Inverse Conway Maneuver

know: Conway's Law as Conway stated it, and the reasoning behind it.
The inverse Conway maneuver and the conditions under which it works or fails.
believe: A change to teams is a change to the product's architecture, and the reverse.
can_do: Predict where a system's awkward interfaces are from its team structure.
Judge whether a planned team reshaping will produce the intended architecture, by checking skills and ownership.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a team structure, the reader predicts where the system's weakest interfaces will be and why.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A company has one iOS team, one Android team and four backend teams split by database. Where would you expect its product to be inconsistent, and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Between platforms for the same feature and across features that span databases, because those are the lines across which design decisions need communication between teams.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter gives at least one case in which the inverse maneuver fails and names the missing condition.
Conway (1968) and Team Topologies are cited for what each contributes; evidence beyond those is labelled as research finding or as the author's experience.

thesis.question: Why do systems end up shaped like the organizations that build them, and when can a leader use that deliberately?
thesis.claim: Systems mirror organizations because every design decision needs communication between the people who make it, so interfaces form where teams talk least; a leader can use this by shaping teams to match the wanted architecture, but the maneuver works only when the new teams hold the skills and the ownership the target boundaries require, and otherwise the old architecture reappears inside the new chart.
thesis.disputed_by: Two opposite views: that architecture is a technical matter architects decide and teams implement, and that redrawing the teams is enough to make the new architecture follow.
thesis.so_what: A leader reviews a team change as an architecture change and an architecture change as a team change, and checks skills and ownership before announcing either.
thesis.how_why: Conway's argument is about the cost of communication: two parts designed by people who do not talk get a narrow, slow-changing interface. The inverse maneuver changes who talks, but code, knowledge and operational duty stay where they were unless they are moved too.

supporting_claims.claim: Conway's argument holds: organizing a design effort is already a design decision, and two parts of a system get an interface only where their designers negotiate one, so the system's structure copies the organization's communication structure.

Because a design decision across a team line costs more than one inside a team, software interfaces on team lines come out narrow, duplicated or queued, which makes a system's weak interfaces predictable from its team structure.

A leader can use the law deliberately by shaping teams to match the wanted architecture, the inverse Conway maneuver, which makes every team design an architecture decision and every architecture decision a request to the organization.
The maneuver works only when each new team holds the skills and the ownership its boundary requires; when either is missing, the old architecture reappears inside the new chart.

Both opposite views fail: architecture decided apart from the teams is overruled by the communication structure, and teams redrawn without moving skills and ownership change the chart and not the system.

role.contribution: Shows why the arrangement of teams, and not only their quality, decides the shape of what is built.

additional_patterns.applies_to: what-conway-argued, where-teams-talk-least, predict-weak-interfaces: the law before its mechanism, the mechanism before the prediction that uses it; the-inverse-maneuver before skills-and-ownership

flow.rationale: After the opening callouts of the page format, the reader meets a product whose faults sit on team lines, so the law arrives as the explanation of something already seen. Conway's argument comes before the cost mechanism because the mechanism is a reading of it, and the prediction pattern comes after both because it is the mechanism run forward on a structure; placed first it would be a rule of thumb without a reason. The inverse maneuver follows the prediction because it is the same law used to choose a structure where the prediction only read one, and its two conditions follow it at once so that the reader never holds the maneuver without its limits. The two mistakes come after the maneuver and its conditions because the first ignores the law the maneuver uses and the second ignores the conditions; shown earlier, the second could not be told from the maneuver itself. The trade-offs come after the mistakes because each mistake moves only one side of a mismatch, and a table of choices shown before them would present those one-sided moves as options without their failure. The worked example comes after all of it because it needs the conditions to tell Corvane's working change from its failing one, and the AI section is a coda that asks whether the mechanism survives a change in who writes the code.

hook.content: In 2021 a customer of Corvane could have drawn Corvane's team structure without ever seeing it. The office application and the mobile app each behaved consistently, and they disagreed with each other about whether a technician could take a second job inside a travel-time window. The product was sound inside each team's part and broken exactly on the line between two teams.

bridge.from_reader_world: A reader who builds software has used a product in which the web and mobile versions of one feature behave differently, and has probably guessed that two teams built them.
bridge.to_topic: That guess is Conway's Law, and this chapter shows why it holds and what a leader can do with it.

thesis_statement.text: Systems mirror organizations because every design decision needs communication between the people who make it, so interfaces form where teams talk least. A leader can use this by shaping teams to match the wanted architecture, but the maneuver works only when the new teams hold the skills and the ownership the target boundaries require; otherwise the old architecture reappears inside the new chart.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

roadmap.placement: IN THIS CHAPTER callout and the second lead paragraph (p02)

promises.promise: See a product whose faults sit on its team lines.
Learn Conway's Law as Conway argued it, and the evidence for it.
Understand the cost of communication that makes interfaces form where teams talk least.
Predict a system's weak interfaces from its team structure.
Use the inverse Conway maneuver, and check the two conditions it depends on.
Recognize the two opposite mistakes and weigh the alternatives to the maneuver.
See three team changes at Corvane checked against the conditions, and what AI changes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2021 a customer of Corvane could have drawn Corvane's team structure from its product alone, because the product was consistent inside each application and inconsistent exactly where one team's work met another's.

evidence.what: The Two Calendars, 2021, at 50 people: the office application built by Web and the mobile app built by Mobile gave different answers to whether a technician could take a second job inside a travel-time window; each application agreed with itself.
evidence.shows: The fault lay on the line between two teams and nowhere inside either.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Systems mirror organizations because every design decision needs communication between the people who make it, so a leader can shape teams to get a wanted architecture, but only when skills and ownership move with them; the chapter goes from the case, through Conway's argument and the mechanism behind it, to predicting weak interfaces, then to the inverse Conway maneuver and its two conditions, the two opposite mistakes, the trade-offs, Corvane's three team changes, and AI.

transition_in.carries_over: A product whose faults sat on team lines.
transition_in.introduces: The law that explains it, the use a leader can make of it, and the route through the chapter.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene: Faults on the Team Lines
sections.controlling_idea: Corvane's product in 2021 and 2022 was inconsistent only where two teams' work met, and the people who built it were not careless.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the case the law has to explain: faults located on team lines.

flow.rationale: Structure first, then the two faults in the order they happened, then the question; with the question first the reader would not yet see that the faults share a location.

transition_in.carries_over: The lead's short account of a product that showed its team structure.
transition_in.introduces: The structure, the two faults and where each one sat.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2021 Corvane had four teams, each of which owned one part of the product and built it well.

evidence.what: 50 people, 28 in product and tech; Web (office application), Mobile (technicians' app), Integrations (billing and stock connections), Core (shared services), under two engineering managers.
evidence.shows: Sets out the structure the product will be compared with.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Both faults Corvane's customers saw in 2021 and 2022 sat on a line between two teams: the overlapping-jobs rule between Web and Mobile, and the job-status rule between Mobile and Integrations.

evidence.what: Two Calendars (2021): planners and technicians saw different schedules for three weeks. Second Calendar (2022): a job marked complete on the phone stayed open in billing exports for eleven days.
evidence.shows: Two faults, two team lines, and no fault of this kind inside any one team's application.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: Four teams that each built their part well.
transition_in.introduces: Where the product nevertheless failed.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The pattern is too regular to be carelessness: each team's code was correct by that team's reading of the rule, so the question is why the product was weak exactly where the teams met.

evidence.what: If the cause were individual error, faults would be spread through the product; they were confined to the places where two teams' work met.
evidence.shows: Turns the case into the question the chapter answers.

transition_in.carries_over: Two faults on two team lines.
transition_in.introduces: What that regularity rules out, and the question it leaves.

sections.heading: Conway's Law: What Conway Argued in 1968
sections.controlling_idea: Conway argued that an organization that designs a system produces a design whose structure copies the organization's communication structure, because organizing the work is already a design decision and because two parts get an interface only where their designers negotiate one.

advances_thesis.how: States the law in its author's terms and gives his two-step reasoning, his examples and the evidence since.

flow.rationale: The law is stated first so the reader knows what is being argued for; the two steps of reasoning follow in the order in which one depends on the other; the example and the study come last because they are read as confirmations of an argument already understood.

transition_in.carries_over: The question why a product is weak where teams meet.
transition_in.introduces: The answer Melvin Conway gave in 1968.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Conway's Law, as Conway stated it in 1968, is that organizations which design systems are constrained to produce designs that are copies of their communication structures.

evidence.what: Conway's conclusion: "organizations which design systems (in the broad sense used here) are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations." Published in Datamation, April 1968. The paper supplements the author's own sources; it was read for this chapter.
evidence.shows: Gives the law in its author's words, and marks that he says communication structure and not org chart.
evidence.source: Melvin E. Conway, "How Do Committees Invent?", Datamation, April 1968 (read at melconway.com)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The first step of Conway's reasoning is that organizing a design effort is itself a design decision: once the work is divided among groups, the designs that would need other communication paths can no longer be pursued.

evidence.what: Conway: the act of organizing a design team means certain design decisions have already been made, explicitly or otherwise; each delegation narrows the class of design alternatives that can be effectively pursued. Team Topologies highlights the same passage.
evidence.shows: The structure of the system is partly chosen when the teams are chosen, before any design discussion.
evidence.source: Melvin E. Conway, "How Do Committees Invent?", Datamation, April 1968 (read at melconway.com)

transition_in.carries_over: The law as stated.
transition_in.introduces: The first of the two steps that lead to it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The second step is that two parts of a system can work together only through an interface, and an interface exists only where the designers of the two parts have negotiated and agreed one, so the map of the system's parts and the map of who talks to whom have the same shape.

evidence.what: Conway: where two nodes of the system are connected, the two design groups must have negotiated and agreed upon an interface specification; he calls the structure-preserving relationship a homomorphism. Team Topologies calls its pull the "homomorphic force".
evidence.shows: Explains the copying: every connection in the system stands for a conversation between groups.
evidence.source: Melvin E. Conway, "How Do Committees Invent?", Datamation, April 1968 (read at melconway.com)

transition_in.carries_over: The division of work as a design decision.
transition_in.introduces: What the division does to the connections between parts.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Conway's own examples show the copying in miniature: eight people asked to write two compilers, split five and three, produced a five-phase compiler and a three-phase compiler.

evidence.what: A contract research organization assigned five people to a COBOL compiler and three to an ALGOL compiler; the COBOL compiler ran in five phases and the ALGOL compiler in three.
evidence.shows: The number of parts followed the number of people, not the nature of the problem.
evidence.source: Melvin E. Conway, "How Do Committees Invent?", Datamation, April 1968 (read at melconway.com)

transition_in.carries_over: The argument in the abstract.
transition_in.introduces: Conway's concrete case.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Since 1968 the law has been tested at least once with measurement: a study of matched software products found the product of the loosely coupled organization more modular in every pair, with the limits its authors state.

evidence.what: Research finding: MacCormack, Rusnak and Baldwin compared five matched pairs of software products, one open source and one commercial each, by propagation cost (the share of the system a change to one element can affect, on average); in all five pairs the open-source product was more modular, by up to a factor of eight. Stated limits: five pairs, software only, and two rival causal explanations (designs evolve to reflect their environment, or designers choose modularity on purpose).
evidence.shows: Independent support for mirroring, with its strength and limits stated; labelled as a research finding beyond the two main sources.
evidence.source: Alan MacCormack, John Rusnak and Carliss Baldwin, "Exploring the Duality between Product and Organizational Architectures: A Test of the Mirroring Hypothesis", Harvard Business School Working Paper 08-039 (revised 2011)

transition_in.carries_over: Conway's argument and examples, which are reasoning and anecdote.
transition_in.introduces: A measured test and what it does and does not establish.

sections.heading: Why Interfaces Form Where Teams Talk Least
sections.controlling_idea: The force behind the law is the cost of communication: a design decision inside a team is cheap to make and to revisit, one across a team line is expensive, so software interfaces on team lines are narrow, slow to change, duplicated or queued.

advances_thesis.how: Turns Conway's argument into a mechanism a leader can reason with.

flow.rationale: The software interface is defined before the cost argument that uses it; the three outcomes follow the cost argument directly because each is a result of the cost, and they answer the opening question about Corvane's two faults; the warning about which lines count comes last because it qualifies everything before it and is the first thing the prediction pattern of the next section needs.

transition_in.carries_over: Conway's claim that the system copies the communication structure.
transition_in.introduces: The cost that makes it do so, and the forms the copy takes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two kinds of interface have to be kept apart, the software interface between two parts of a system and the team interface of chapter 1, and Conway's claim is that they coincide.

evidence.what: The introduction defines interface as the software kind; chapter 1's kind, the agreed way work and knowledge cross between teams, is called a team interface in this chapter; a software interface whose sides disagree or that changes too slowly is called weak.
evidence.shows: Keeps one sense per term before the mechanism uses both.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A design decision made inside a team costs a conversation at a desk and can be revisited the next day, while the same decision across a team line costs a meeting, a document and a wait, so teams make as few of those as they can.

evidence.what: The author's reading of Conway's argument as a cost of communication: decisions that are cheap get made often and corrected; decisions that are expensive get made once, narrowly, or not at all.
evidence.shows: Explains why the parts of a system owned by one team fit together and the parts owned by two do not.

transition_in.carries_over: Two kinds of interface that coincide.
transition_in.introduces: Why they coincide: what a decision costs on each side of a team line.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An expensive decision at a team line ends in one of three ways: a narrow contract that rarely changes, the same logic built twice, or a queue at the team that owns what others need; both of Corvane's faults were the second.

evidence.what: Outcome | What you see in the software | What you see in the organization | Corvane. Narrow contract: a small, stable API | little cross-team talk, and it is enough | Core's service API in 2021. Duplicate: the same rule implemented in two places | each team decides alone | the overlapping-jobs rule in Web and Mobile, 2021. Queue: one path every change must take | requests wait at one team | none in 2021; the worked example shows one from 2023. The lead-in names the narrow contract as the good outcome and Chapter 1's failure pattern The Unowned Interface for the duplicate.
evidence.shows: Gives the three shapes a weak or strong interface can take, each with a Corvane instance.

transition_in.carries_over: Decisions across a team line are expensive.
transition_in.introduces: The three results of that expense.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: What counts is who actually talks, not who reports to whom: Conway wrote of communication structure, and Team Topologies warns that the org chart does not show it.

evidence.what: Conway's law names the communication structure; Team Topologies treats the org chart as a poor picture of how teams communicate. The author's working record is [[org-chart-problems]].
evidence.shows: Stops the reader from reading the law off reporting lines.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: Three outcomes at a team line.
transition_in.introduces: Which lines count as team lines: those of real communication, not of reporting.

sections.heading: Pattern: Predict the Weak Interfaces from the Team Structure
sections.controlling_idea: Given a team structure, a leader can predict where the product will be inconsistent or slow by listing the things users experience as one and marking every team line each of them crosses.

advances_thesis.how: Makes the law a diagnostic the reader can run on a structure.

flow.rationale: Procedure, then its results on common cases, then its limit; the limit comes last because it qualifies results the reader has to have seen.

transition_in.carries_over: Three outcomes at a team line.
transition_in.introduces: A way to find the lines that matter before the incidents do.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The prediction has three steps: list what users experience as one thing, mark each team line it crosses, and ask at each line whether a contract exists and who owns it.

evidence.what: User of the pattern: the leader or architect reviewing a team structure. Outcome measure: the share of cross-team incidents and delays in the following two quarters that fall on lines the review marked.
evidence.shows: Names the pattern's user and how to know the prediction was worth making, as the book requires of every pattern.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Common team structures have predictable weak interfaces, because each puts its lines across a different thing that users experience as one.

evidence.what: Teams cut by | Line runs across | Expect. Client platform (web, each mobile platform) | every feature that exists on more than one client | the same feature behaving differently per client. Technical layer or data store (front end, back end, one team per database) | every feature that needs more than one layer or store | slow features, and data that disagrees between stores. Product area with one shared release or infrastructure team | every launch | a queue at the shared team. Site or time zone | whatever is split between sites | an interface at the site line, however the code is organized.
evidence.shows: Lets the reader apply the prediction to structures they know; each row follows from where decisions need communication between teams.

transition_in.carries_over: The three steps.
transition_in.introduces: What they yield for four common structures.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The prediction says where to look and not that something is broken: a line with an owned contract and little need for change is a good interface, and the law is why it is good.

evidence.what: Team Topologies: not all communication is good; if two teams should not need to communicate according to the software design and do, something is wrong. The author's working record is [[conways-law]].
evidence.shows: A team line is a weakness only where a decision that keeps changing has to cross it.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: Predicted weak interfaces.
transition_in.introduces: The limit of the prediction: lines that are fine.

sections.heading: Pattern: The Inverse Conway Maneuver
sections.controlling_idea: The inverse Conway maneuver uses the law on purpose: decide the architecture you want, then shape the teams so that the cheap conversations happen inside each wanted part and the expensive ones only across the wanted interfaces.

advances_thesis.how: Introduces the deliberate use of the law and what it makes of team design.

transition_in.carries_over: A law that predicts where a structure will hurt.
transition_in.introduces: The same law used to choose the structure.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The inverse Conway maneuver is to choose the architecture first and then shape the teams to match it, so that the structure the organization naturally produces is the one you want.

evidence.what: Team Topologies describes the maneuver under the name reverse Conway maneuver and carries the line that team assignments are the first draft of the architecture. User of the pattern: the leaders who decide team boundaries, with the architects. Outcome measure: whether a change inside one wanted part can be made and released by one team without waiting for another.
evidence.shows: Defines the maneuver, credits it, and names its user and outcome measure.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019); author's notes

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The maneuver makes team design an architecture decision, so the people who draw teams are deciding architecture whether or not they know it, and technical leaders belong in the room.

evidence.what: Team Topologies argues that managers who decide which teams build which services are implicitly deciding the system architecture, and that deciding the shape and boundaries of teams without input from technical leaders is very ineffective.
evidence.shows: The consequence for who takes part in an organizational decision.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: Teams shaped to produce an architecture.
transition_in.introduces: Who therefore has to take part in shaping them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The reverse holds too: an architecture decision is a request to the organization, and Team Topologies turns Conway's law into a standing question about which better designs the current teams cannot reach.

evidence.what: Team Topologies: the law "creates an imperative to keep asking: 'Is there a better design that is not available to us because of our organization?'"
evidence.shows: An architecture that needs conversations the organization does not have will not be built as drawn.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: A team change is an architecture change.
transition_in.introduces: An architecture change is a team change.

sections.heading: The Two Conditions: Skills and Ownership
sections.controlling_idea: The maneuver changes who talks to whom, but code, knowledge and operational duty stay where they were unless they are moved too, so it works only when each new team holds the skills and the ownership its boundary requires.

advances_thesis.how: States the conditions and gives a failing case with the missing condition named.

flow.rationale: What the maneuver leaves in place comes first because both conditions are derived from it; skills before ownership because a team cannot own what it cannot change; the failure case last because it needs both conditions to be diagnosed.

transition_in.carries_over: The maneuver as designed.
transition_in.introduces: What it does not move, and the two conditions that follow.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Redrawing teams changes who sits and plans together, and it leaves three things where they were: the code, the knowledge of how it works, and the duty to run it.

evidence.what: Mermaid decision flow, top to bottom: 'Wanted architecture' → 'Teams redrawn to match' → 'Does each team hold the skills its boundary needs?' → (no) 'Old architecture reappears inside the new chart'; (yes) → 'Does each team own its code, its decisions and its operation?' → (no) the same failure node; (yes) → 'Architecture follows the teams'.
evidence.shows: Shows the two checks standing between a redrawn chart and a changed architecture.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The skills condition is that each new team can design, change, release and operate its part without borrowing a person from another team; where it cannot, the team that holds the missing skill becomes a party to every change.

evidence.what: The author's reading of Conway's argument: a dependency on someone else's skill is a communication path, so the old interface is still there. Team Topologies makes skills an input to team design ('Given our skills, constraints, cultural and engineering maturity, desired software architecture, and business goals, which team topology...').
evidence.shows: Why a team without the skill does not really have the boundary the chart gives it.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: Three things a redrawn chart leaves in place.
transition_in.introduces: The first condition, about knowledge.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ownership condition is that every part of the system is owned by exactly one team, which holds its code, the decisions about it and the duty to operate it.

evidence.what: Team Topologies: "Every part of the software system needs to be owned by exactly one team." Other teams may propose changes; they do not make them.
evidence.shows: A boundary on the chart without ownership of code, decisions and operation leaves the old owner in every change.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: The skills condition.
transition_in.introduces: The second condition, about code, decisions and operation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: When either condition is missing the old architecture reappears inside the new chart, as when a system is split into services by team and every service still shares one database.

evidence.what: Condition | What has to move with the team | Sign that it did not | What reappears. Skills | knowledge of the domain, the code, releasing and running it | changes wait for one person in another team | the old team, as a queue. Ownership | code, decision rights, on-call | several teams change the same code or schema; nobody is paged | the old system, with more meetings.
evidence.shows: Summarizes both conditions as checks a leader can run.

evidence.what: Team Topologies' joined-at-the-database monolith: several applications or services all coupled to the same database schema; and the distributed monolith, where almost every change requires other services to change. Missing condition: ownership of the data.
evidence.shows: A named failing case of the maneuver: teams and services were redrawn, the shared schema was not divided, and the single system survived.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019); author's notes

transition_in.carries_over: Two conditions.
transition_in.introduces: What happens without them, with a case.

sections.heading: Anti-Patterns: Two Opposite Mistakes
sections.controlling_idea: The law is ignored in two opposite ways: architecture designed apart from the teams, and teams redrawn in the belief that the architecture will follow.

advances_thesis.how: Answers the two views the thesis is disputed by.

transition_in.carries_over: The maneuver done with its conditions.
transition_in.introduces: The two common ways of doing without them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The first mistake treats architecture as a technical matter that architects decide and teams implement, and the design that results is the one the communication structure allows, not the one drawn.

evidence.what: Team Topologies: "thinking of software architecture as a standalone concept that can be designed in isolation and then implemented by any group of teams is fundamentally wrong."
evidence.shows: The source's verdict on architecture decided apart from team structure.
evidence.source: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019); author's notes

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The second mistake, The Org Chart as Architecture, is the belief that redrawing the teams is enough, and one form of it splits teams ever finer in Conway's name, drawing new team lines across knowledge that is not split with them.

evidence.what: The book's failure pattern The Org Chart as Architecture, and from the author's record [[conways-law]]: many small component teams that multiply handoffs.
evidence.shows: The chart changed and the skills and ownership did not, which is the failing case of the previous section made into a habit.

transition_in.carries_over: Architecture without teams.
transition_in.introduces: Teams without architecture.

sections.heading: Trade-Offs: Move the Teams, Move the Architecture, or Keep the Mismatch
sections.controlling_idea: When teams and architecture disagree there are three choices, and which is right depends on which side is closer to what the product needs and on what moving it costs people.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the conditions under which the maneuver is and is not the right move.

transition_in.carries_over: Two mistakes that each move only one side.
transition_in.introduces: The honest choice among moving one, the other, or neither.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A mismatch between teams and architecture can be closed from either side or kept on purpose, and each choice has a price.

evidence.what: Choice | Right when | Price. Move the teams to the wanted architecture | the architecture is what the product needs and the skills and ownership can move | a reorganization, with its cost to people. Move the architecture to the teams | the teams are well formed around users and the software cuts across them | a migration. Keep the mismatch and own the interface | the area changes rarely, or a change is already planned | a standing contract and a named owner for it.
evidence.shows: Sets the maneuver beside its alternatives.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: None of the three is permanent, because the first design is rarely the best one and the organization has to be able to change when a better one is found.

evidence.what: Conway: "flexibility of organization is important to effective design", because the design that occurs first is almost never the best possible.
evidence.shows: Conway's own conclusion is about keeping the organization able to change, not about finding the final structure.
evidence.source: Melvin E. Conway, "How Do Committees Invent?", Datamation, April 1968 (read at melconway.com)

transition_in.carries_over: Three choices for one mismatch.
transition_in.introduces: Why the choice will have to be made again.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Three Team Changes at Corvane
sections.controlling_idea: Corvane changed its teams three times between 2022 and 2024, and each change did to the architecture what its skills and ownership allowed: one maneuver worked, one failed, and the repair supplied what the failure lacked.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the two conditions to three changes, one that worked and one that failed.

flow.rationale: The table first so that no change is judged before it is shown; then the three changes in the order they happened, which is also success, failure and repair.

transition_in.carries_over: The conditions and trade-offs in general.
transition_in.introduces: Three changes at one company, checked against them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Set side by side, Corvane's three changes to what its teams were or owned differ in what moved with the teams: the skills and the ownership.

evidence.what: Change | Architecture it implied | Skills | Ownership | Result. 2022, 45 engineers in four teams: rules moved into Core | one rule engine, three client applications | Samir Haddad, in Core, understood the scheduling engine and the mobile sync | code in Core; Priya Nambiar decides the rules; Core owns the versioned schema and the weekly rules session | no third incident; Core overloaded. 2023, growing from 45 engineers to 95: eleven product teams and Platform | eleven product areas that change and release separately | launch knowledge stayed with five platform engineers | launches owned by Platform | changes queue for launches; lead time from 4 days to 19. 2024, 95 engineers: a release path a product team runs itself | the same eleven areas | a platform engineer worked inside Scheduling for the first six weeks | Scheduling owns its releases | Scheduling at 6 days; under 7 company-wide three quarters after the brief.
evidence.shows: The same check, skills and ownership, applied to three changes with ledger numbers.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The 2022 change was an inverse maneuver in its smallest form, one boundary moved and no person, and it worked because the team that received the rules already held the skill and was given the code, the decision and the contract.

evidence.what: The 2022 fix: one rule engine in Core; Priya Nambiar, the product manager, decides scheduling and job-status rules; changes published as a versioned schema. No third incident of the kind; Core's six engineers now owned more than they could comfortably understand.
evidence.shows: Both conditions were present, and the architecture followed the teams, at a price paid in Core's load.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: The table as a whole.
transition_in.introduces: Its first row, and why it worked.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The 2023 change failed as a maneuver: the chart drew eleven separately releasable product areas, and because the skill and the ownership of launching stayed in Platform, the architecture did not follow the chart, a team's change still reached customers through another team, and the teams queued for launches.

evidence.what: The Launch Queue, 2024: all eleven product teams needed Platform for some launches and three for every launch; 14 open launch requests; five platform engineers; median lead time from 4 days to 19. Nobody at Corvane had called the 2023 change a maneuver; the chart implied the architecture all the same.
evidence.shows: The failing case with the missing conditions named: release skill and release ownership did not move, so the architecture did not follow the chart.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: A change in which skills and ownership moved.
transition_in.introduces: A change in which neither did.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The 2024 repair did not redraw a single team: it supplied the two missing conditions by rebuilding the release path so that a product team could run it and by moving the skill with a platform engineer, at the price of a migration, and the architecture the 2023 chart had drawn began to exist.

evidence.what: Dario Vance, VP Engineering, and Lena Brandt, who led the platform team: a release path the Scheduling team could run without Platform; a platform engineer worked inside Scheduling for the first six weeks. Scheduling's median lead time 6 days after one quarter; company-wide under 7 three quarters after the brief; the eleven teams were not re-cut.
evidence.shows: Moving skill and ownership, without changing the chart, produced what changing the chart had not.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Corvane, fictional)

transition_in.carries_over: A chart without its conditions.
transition_in.introduces: The conditions supplied, and the result.

sections.heading: What AI Changes Here
sections.controlling_idea: Coding agents lower the cost of writing code on the far side of a team line but not the cost of agreeing what the interface should be, so the mirroring should persist where ownership and review sit.

advances_thesis.how: Tests the chapter's mechanism against agents, with labeled claims.

transition_in.carries_over: A mechanism shown on cases from 2021 to 2024.
transition_in.introduces: Whether it holds when agents write part of the code.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Emerging: in the teams the author has observed, agents write changes in code their team does not own more easily than people did, and those changes still wait for the owning team's review.

evidence.what: Author's observation as of November 2026, labeled Emerging and not a measured result: the writing got cheaper, the agreement did not.
evidence.shows: Gives the basis and the label; the cost Conway's argument rests on is the cost of agreement, which is unchanged.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Speculative: if that holds widely, Conway's Law will describe the structure of ownership and review more than the structure of who writes the code, and weak interfaces will show as review queues at team lines.

evidence.what: Labeled Speculative; it would be confirmed where organizations report that cross-team changes written by agents wait longer for the owner's review than changes written inside the owning team. The argument is taken up in [[where-the-constraint-moves]].
evidence.shows: Marks the claim as reasoning and says what would confirm it.

transition_in.carries_over: Cheaper writing across a team line, unchanged agreement.
transition_in.introduces: What that may do to where the law shows.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: Chapter 1 said teams are components and chapter 2 said whom they are designed for; this chapter adds that the software takes the components' shape, so the two designs are one design, and that the link runs through skills and ownership and not through the chart.
conclusion.so_what: The reader reviews a team change as an architecture change and an architecture change as a team change, and checks skills and ownership before announcing either.

callback.to: The customer who could have drawn Corvane's teams from its product.
callback.how: The reader can now say why the faults sat on the team lines, and what would have to move for a new chart to change the product.

takeaway.content: Before the next team change or architecture change, mark the team lines that the things users experience as one have to cross, and check skills and ownership for each new boundary. The checklist gives the questions.

hand_off.carries_over: Team structure decides architecture, which leaves open how to choose the structure.
hand_off.introduces: The rule for choosing: size ownership by cognitive load and cut along fracture planes.

transition_in.carries_over: The law, the maneuver, its conditions, the worked example and the AI coda.
transition_in.introduces: What holds across the chapter, sorted by how settled it is.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Established: systems copy the communication structure of the organizations that design them, the argument for it is Conway's, a measured study supports it within stated limits, and every part of a system needs exactly one owning team.

Depends on context: whether to move the teams, move the architecture or keep the mismatch depends on which side fits the product and on what can move; and how much a prediction of weak interfaces is worth depends on how often the thing crossing the line changes.
